JSPrismarine / @jsprismarine/entity-brains

@jsprismarine/entity-brains ​

Java Edition's brain AI: memories, sensors, activities, the behavior combinators, and the twenty mobs that build a brain. This is the half of vanilla mob behavior that Bedrock's entity JSON has no way to describe.

typescript
import { BrainMobRegistry, registerBrainMobs } from '@jsprismarine/entity-brains';

const registry = new BrainMobRegistry();
registerBrainMobs(registry); // 20 mobs

const villager = registry.get('minecraft:villager');
const brain = villager.makeBrain({ variant: 'minecraft:farmer' });

// Once per mob tick, in this order, as Java's Mob.customServerAiStep does.
villager.updateActivity(context);
brain.tick(context);

Why this package exists ​

Java runs two unrelated mob AI systems. The goal system is 68 classes and 5520 lines, and 30 of its 67 concrete goal names match a Bedrock minecraft:behavior.* name after snake-casing, so Bedrock's data-driven JSON carries those mobs; @jsprismarine/entity-goals implements them. The brain system is 116 classes and 8905 lines plus 24 sensors, 115 memory modules and 26 activities, and Bedrock publishes no memory, sensor or activity registry at all. A Bedrock-shaped runtime cannot hold the per-mob state a Java brain holds, because the format never names it.

Exactly twenty mob classes build a brain. The list is not a judgement call: scanning the constant pool of every top-level class under net/minecraft/world/entity/ for brainProvider or makeBrain finds 21 classes, and the twenty-first is LivingEntity, which holds the base. Everything else in the game, including every zombie, skeleton, farm animal, slime, guardian and the ender dragon, is goals only.

Two of the twenty carry both systems. Camel and HappyGhast have a registerGoals and a brainProvider, so a server must run both schedulers for them. DUAL_SYSTEM_MOBS reports that list, and BrainMobDefinition.alsoRunsGoals reports it per mob.

docs/research/java-code-only-behavior.md section 4 is the source for the two-system split and for the twenty-mob list.

The source ​

Everything here is read out of the pinned Java Edition 26.3 server jar, which since release 26.1 ships with original class, field and method names and no obfuscation map. The jar is the one @jsprismarine/bedrock-data caches under node_modules/.cache/jsprismarine/java-server/26.3. The villager schedule is the one exception, because Mojang moved it into a datapack: it comes from data/minecraft/timeline/villager_schedule.json in the 26.3 vanilla datapack.

Mobs with a brain2020brainProvider and makeBrain references

All three match. Six of the 115 memory modules register under a name that differs from their Java field name, which is worth knowing when reading a saved brain: NEAREST_LIVING_ENTITIES registers as mobs, NEAREST_VISIBLE_LIVING_ENTITIES as visible_mobs, NEAREST_VISIBLE_ATTACKABLE_PLAYER(S) as nearest_visible_targetable_player(s), LONG_JUMP_COOLDOWN_TICKS as long_jump_cooling_down, BREEZE_SHOOT_RECOVERING as breeze_shoot_recover, and LIKED_NOTEBLOCK_POSITION as liked_noteblock.

The brain model ​

A brain is a memory map, a sensor list, and a table of behaviors keyed by priority and activity. One tick runs four steps in Java's order: age the memories, run the sensors, start every stopped behavior whose activity is active, then tick every running one. Starting before ticking is observable, because a behavior started this tick also ticks this tick.

Memories ​

A memory is a typed slot holding an optional value with an optional expiry in ticks. Three rules decide most of what a brain does.

A memory set with a time to live of n is readable on n ticks and is cleared on the n plus first, because MemorySlot.tick checks expiry before decrementing.

An empty array is stored as no value. Brain.setMemory nulls out an empty collection, which is why value_present on a list memory means "the sensor found something" rather than "the sensor ran".

An unregistered memory fails every precondition, including registered. A brain only registers the memories its declared list, its sensors and its behaviors name, so a behavior whose memories the mob never declared is silently inert. That is the mechanism behind several vanilla quirks, including why WardenAi.setDigCooldown checks that the memory already has a value before writing it.

Memory preconditions ​

MemoryStatus has three members. value_present and value_absent are the obvious ones. registered means the slot must exist but may be empty, and a behavior asks for it when it intends to write the memory, which is how the brain learns to allocate the slot.

Activities ​

A brain is in exactly one non-core activity at a time plus every core activity, and core is the only core activity any vanilla mob declares. The brain itself never chooses an activity: it only answers whether one is possible. The choice lives in each mob's updateActivity, which calls setActiveActivityToFirstValid with an ordered list, and that list is the mob's priority order between activities.

Leaving an activity erases the memories it declared as memoriesToEraseWhenStopped, which is the ActivityData.create(activity, priority, list, memory) shorthand Java uses for ATTACK_TARGET, AVOID_TARGET, ADMIRING_ITEM and friends.

Behaviors ​

BehaviorControl has four members: tryStart, tickOrStop, doStop and a status that is stopped or running. Behavior adds memory preconditions and a duration drawn from [minDuration, maxDuration], and its canStillUse returns false by default, so a behavior that does not override it runs for exactly one tick.

OneShot is a behavior whose whole body is one function that reports whether it did anything. Nearly all of Java's behavior library is built this way, through BehaviorBuilder.

The declarative form ​

Java writes BehaviorBuilder as an applicative functor over MemoryCondition, because DataFixerUpper gave it one for free. The content is simpler than the encoding, and this package writes it as a fluent chain that accumulates the accessor types.

typescript
const setLookTarget = behavior('SetEntityLookTarget')
    .absent(MemoryModuleTypes.LOOK_TARGET)
    .present(MemoryModuleTypes.NEAREST_VISIBLE_LIVING_ENTITIES)
    .build((context, lookTarget, nearest) => {
        const target = nearest.get().findClosest(predicate);
        if (target === undefined) return false;
        lookTarget.set(entityTracker(target));
        return true;
    });

The combinators ​

GateBehavior runs a weighted list of children under one set of memory conditions. Its order policy is ordered or shuffled and its running policy is run_one or try_all, and it stops once no child is running. RunOne is the shuffled run_one case and is the most used combinator in the game. TriggerGate is the same over plain triggers rather than full behaviors, so nothing stays running across ticks.

The shuffle is the exponential ranking trick Java uses. Each entry takes the key -random ** (1 / weight) and the list sorts ascending, which makes the chance an entry sorts first proportional to its weight.

A few of these are worth calling out.

The goat is inverted. Its idle activity requires RAM_COOLDOWN_TICKS and LONG_JUMP_COOLDOWN_TICKS to be present, so a goat is idle precisely while it is still waiting out its timers. GoatAi.initMemories fills both on spawn.

The happy ghast's panic activity has no behaviors at all. It exists so that IS_PANICKING suppresses every idle behavior while the core activity's AnimalPanic flies the ghast away.

The frog splits one wander three ways. idle, swim and lay_spawn do nearly the same thing and are told apart by IS_IN_WATER, IS_PREGNANT and LONG_JUMP_MID_JUMP. None of those three has a Bedrock equivalent.

The warden never gives up on an unreachable target. Its StopAttackingIfTargetInvalid is built with canGrowTiredOfTryingToReachTarget false, where every other mob drops a target it has not reached in 200 ticks.

The creaking's activity choice is overridden outside the table. CreakingAi.updateActivity falls back to the default activity whenever the creaking cannot move, which is how a watched creaking freezes mid-chase.

The zoglin has no <Mob>Ai class. Its three activities are static methods on Zoglin itself, which is why a scan for *Ai.class finds nineteen files for twenty mobs.

The villager schedule ​

The villager is the only brain mob with a schedule, and in 26.1 Mojang moved it out of code into the minecraft:timeline datapack type. VILLAGER_SCHEDULE and BABY_VILLAGER_SCHEDULE are the two tracks of data/minecraft/timeline/villager_schedule.json.

TickAdultBaby
10idleidle
2000work
3000play
6000idle
9000meet
10000play
11000idle
12000restrest

Brain.updateActivityFromSchedule reads the schedule at most once every twenty ticks, which is Brain.SCHEDULE_UPDATE_DELAY. The throttle is observable: a villager crossing a keyframe can take up to a second to notice.

The warden's anger ​

AngerManagement is per-suspect anger that decays by one a tick, clamped at 150, with three bands at 0, 40 and 80. A plain disturbance adds 35, so it takes three to make a warden angry. A projectile adds 10. Being hit adds ANGRY's minimum plus 20.

The sort is the part worth reading. A suspect the warden is already angry at outranks one it is not, a player outranks a non-player in the same band, and only then does the raw anger decide. That is why a warden chases the player who poked it rather than the skeleton that shot it, even when the skeleton has more anger.

Anger is not a memory and does not live in the brain. A host owns the AngerManagement and passes it to makeWardenBrain, because the anger outlives any one brain.

The piglin's gold economy ​

wantsToPickUp is the rule, and reading it in order is the clearest statement of the economy. Repellents are never picked up. A baby skips the items in #minecraft:ignored_by_piglin_babies. A gold ingot is taken only when the off hand is free. Food is taken only when the piglin has not eaten recently. Anything else goes by whether it beats what the piglin already holds.

Being handed a gold ingot holds ADMIRING_ITEM for 119 ticks, which is ADMIRE_DURATION, and that memory is what puts the piglin into the admire_item activity. onBarter is the hook makePiglinBrain takes so the host can roll its data-defined barter table after admiration ends.

Four memories decide what admiring does, and none of them has a Bedrock equivalent: ADMIRING_ITEM, TIME_TRYING_TO_REACH_ADMIRE_ITEM, DISABLE_WALK_TO_ADMIRE_ITEM and ADMIRING_DISABLED. The third is the interesting one. A piglin that spends 200 ticks failing to reach an item gives up and refuses to path to one for another 200, but still wants an item that lands in front of it.

The BrainWorld seam ​

Java's behaviors reach straight into ServerLevel, Mob, PathNavigation and PoiManager. This package keeps none of those. Everything a behavior or a sensor needs from outside the brain arrives through three interfaces in src/world.ts.

BrainWorld is the level: the clock, the random source, the entities and items nearby, the targeting tests, blocks and block tags, a block search, points of interest with claim and release, a random reachable position, sounds and game events.

BrainMob is the body: its brain, its navigation, a condition writer, look, jump, attack, a sound, and an attribute lookup.

BrainNavigation is path following: moveTo, isDone, isStuck, canReach and stop. This is deliberately this package's own interface and not an import. @jsprismarine/entity-goals owns the 170 Bedrock goals and an A* path finder over its own NavigationView, and a server satisfies both interfaces with one adapter over that finder. Depending on entity-goals here would make the brain system wait on the goal system, and the two are independent.

Two members do more work than their size suggests. BrainWorld.randomPos stands in for Java's whole ai/util tree, nine classes (LandRandomPos, AirRandomPos, AirAndWaterRandomPos, DefaultRandomPos, HoverRandomPos and their helpers) whose only job is to draw a reachable position subject to a medium and a direction. BrainEntity.conditions is a string set that answers every boolean fact Java reads off a concrete mob class, such as Armadillo::isScared or Camel::refuseToMove; EntityCondition names the ones this package reads. That mirrors how @jsprismarine/entities keeps its filter view small, and it means a host that cannot answer a fact simply leaves it out.

The test double ​

src/testWorld.ts carries TestWorld, TestMob, TestEntity, TestItemEntity and TestNavigation. It is a real implementation, not a mock: entities, blocks, points of interest and the clock are plain data a test writes, and every member answers from that data. Tests script the random source rather than seeding it, so a draw is a fact of the test.

typescript
const world = new TestWorld({ dayTime: 2000 });
world.addPoi({ x: 2, y: 64, z: 0 }, 'minecraft:farmer');

const body = world.spawn('minecraft:villager', { x: 0, y: 64, z: 0 });
body.attach(VILLAGER_BRAIN.makeBrain({ variant: 'minecraft:farmer' }));

VILLAGER_BRAIN.updateActivity(body.context);
body.tickBrain();

TestNavigation records every moveTo and lets a test mark a position unreachable, which is how the CANT_REACH_WALK_TARGET_SINCE path is exercised without a path finder.

What is covered and what is partial ​

The brain core, the activity stack, the memory model, the combinators and all 24 sensors are complete. All twenty mobs have their real activity table, their real priorities, their real memory conditions and their real constants, and the brain runs them.

The behavior library is 37 shared behaviors in src/behavior/common.ts plus the mob-specific ones beside each mob. A behavior whose effect is expressible through the seam is implemented in full. The rest keep their real name, their real memory conditions and their real constants, and they do the memory bookkeeping Java does, while leaving the world effect to the host. Those are the behaviors that need facts the seam deliberately does not carry.

  • Inventories and items. The allay's delivery needs its inventory, and the copper golem's transfer needs two containers. Piglin bartering uses makePiglinBrain's onBarter hook so the host can roll the active minecraft:barter table; the allay and copper golem write their memories and leave the item move to the host.
  • Block effects. The frog's TryLaySpawnOnFluidNearLand leaves block placement to the host. The sniffer checks minecraft:sniffer_diggable_block, drops Java's digging loot after 120 ticks, and remembers a position only after a successful dig. Java does not change the block.
  • Damage and projectiles. The warden fires its sonic boom after a 34-tick windup. The host applies 10 sonic_boom damage, which bypasses armor and armor enchantments, then applies the 15-by-20-block range and resistance-scaled knockback. The breeze's wind charge still leaves its projectile effect to the host.
  • Villager professions and trading. VillagerProfession carries only what the brain reads: the profession id, its job-site point of interest and its secondary blocks. WorkAtComposter, HarvestFarmland, UseBonemeal, ShowTradesToPlayer, TradeWithVillager, GiveGiftToHero and VillagerMakeLove are present by name with their real priorities and weights, and their effects belong to @jsprismarine/trading and the farming code.
  • Raids. The villager brain reads raid status from its host and requests bell, sky-seeking, celebration, and reset effects through that seam. The host still owns raid creation, waves, and victory state; this server does not start pillager patrols or village raids.
  • Poses and animations. A behavior that sets a pose in Java writes an EntityCondition here instead, so a host can drive its own animation state.

Two deliberate simplifications are worth naming. AnimalMakeLove writes only the body's own BREED_TARGET, because a partner is a BrainEntity view rather than a second brain; a host that wants Java's symmetric pairing writes the partner's memory itself. GoToWantedItem always declares WALK_TARGET as registered and refuses in its body when a walk is already running, where Java picks registered or absent from its interruptOngoingWalk argument; the behavior is the same and it keeps one builder chain instead of two with different accessor shapes.

Tests ​

The tests cover the memory expiry rule and the precondition map, the activity stack and the schedule throttle, each combinator, each of the 24 sensors against the world double, and one representative situation for each of the twenty mobs: an idle villager going to work at tick 2000 and staying idle without a job site, a piglin holding ADMIRING_ITEM for 119 ticks when given gold, a warden escalating through 0, 40 and 80, a frog targeting a slime and switching to tongue, and the camel and the happy ghast ticking their brain beside a goal scheduler double.

Where a constant matters, the test title or a comment names it and says where it came from.

sh
pnpm --filter @jsprismarine/entity-brains exec vitest run

Brain ​

Defined in: brain.ts:120

One mob's memories, sensors and activity table. Java's Brain.

A tick runs every sensor, ages every memory slot, starts the stopped behaviors of the active activities in ascending priority order, then ticks the running ones. The brain never picks an activity itself; the mob's updateActivity does that, and the brain only reports whether an activity's conditions hold.

Defined in: behavior/gate.ts:69

ShufflingList ​

Defined in: behavior/gate.ts:21

Java's ShufflingList: a weighted list that reorders in place.

The draw is the exponential ranking trick Java uses: each entry takes the key -random ** (1 / weight) and the list sorts ascending, which makes the probability that a given entry sorts first proportional to its weight.

WardenEntitySensor ​

Defined in: sensing/sensors.ts:520

Java's WardenEntitySensor: NearestLivingEntitySensor plus one extra memory.

NEAREST_ATTACKABLE goes to the closest targetable player, and only to the closest non-player when there is no player at all. That ordering is why a warden prefers a player standing further away over a mob at its feet.

EntityConditions ​

EntityConditions = ReadonlySet<string>

Defined in: world.ts:94

The boolean facts about a mob that Java reads off the concrete mob class rather than off the brain, such as Armadillo::isScared or Camel::refuseToMove.

They live in one set rather than in one accessor each for the same reason @jsprismarine/entities keeps its filter view small: one member answers every one of them, and a host that cannot answer one simply leaves it out. EntityCondition names the ones this package reads.

VILLAGER_SCHEDULE ​

const VILLAGER_SCHEDULE: Schedule

Defined in: mobs/villager.ts:88

The villager schedule, read from data/minecraft/timeline/villager_schedule.json in the 26.3 vanilla datapack.

An adult works from 2000 to 9000, meets from 9000 to 11000, idles until 12000 and rests after. The first keyframe is at tick 10, not 0, so the very start of the day is the previous day's last activity.

animalPanic() ​

animalPanic(speedMultiplier, options?): BehaviorControl

Defined in: behavior/common.ts:112

Java's AnimalPanic.

It runs for 100 to 120 ticks, holds IS_PANICKING for its whole duration, and redraws a flee position each time the navigation finishes. The entry conditions are REGISTERED rather than present, so the behavior itself decides whether to run: it starts when HURT_BY is a damage type in the tag or when something else already set IS_PANICKING.
